30.63315,-97.67324: Negro Fine Arts School Twenty years before the integration of the Georgetown public school district, a progressive music professor and her three students embarked on a program to explore a new musical teaching theory and give African American children a chance to learn music. 30.63449,-97.67581: Jessie Daniel Ames. (1883-1972) A native of Palestine, Texas, Jessie Daniel came to Georgetown in 1893. She graduated from Southwestern University in 1902. 30.63662,-97.67742: Judge Greenleaf Fisk. (May 19, 1807 - Jan. 26, 1888) Born in Albany, New York, Greenleaf Fisk was the son of a Presbyterian minister. 30.63666,-97.67723: Williamson County. Created March 13, 1848, and organized by a special committee approved by Gov. George T. 30.63668,-97.67735: Chief Justice John Edward Hickman. (1883-1962) A distinguished chief justice of the Texas Supreme Court, and a native of Williamson County. 30.9107,-97.55241: Odle Log Cabin. A native of Tennessee, pioneer John Odle (1824-1913) moved to Texas in 1843, one year after his marriage to Lucinda Reeder (d. 1890). 30.93617,-97.54032: Main Street Bridges. A number of bridges have been built over Salado Creek on Main Street since 1870. (1986) #3189
30.93815,-97.53162: Capt. Milton Wesley Damron. Milton Wesley Damron (1825-1887), an early settler and Salado public servant, was born in Tennessee and came to Texas as part of the Mercer Colony. (2006) #13676
30.93819,-97.53199: Robert Bonner Halley. A native of Georgia, Robert B. Halley brought his family to this area about 1853. With partner T.J. Eubanks, he operated a liquor distillery and a flour and grist mill on the Lampasas River. 30.93929,-97.53206: Salado Cemetery. Established 1856 on 2.5-acre site given by E.S.C. Robertson. Distinguished Texans interred here include the Rev. G.W. 30.9415,-97.53008: Major A.J. Rose House. Built in 1870-72, this structure typifies the Greek Revival style with its symmetrical facade. Major Archibald Johnson Rose. (1830-1903) Before migrating to Texas, A. J. Rose made a fortune in the 1849 California Gold Rush. 30.94274,-97.52766: Salado United Methodist Church. In 1854, the Rev. Thomas Gilmore, a Methodist circuit rider, led a revival at Pecan Grove on the north side of Salado Creek. 30.9431,-97.52868: Salado Methodist Church. Building erected 1890 for a congregation organized 1854 at site on Salado Creek. Circuit riders serving congregation included the Rev. J.E. 30.94365,-97.54004: Robertson Home. Built by Col. E.S.C. Robertson and wife, Mary Elizabeth (Dickey). 30.94366,-97.53774: Stagecoach Inn. Constructed during the 1860s, the Stagecoach Inn was known as Salado Hotel and as Shady Villa before the current name was adopted in 1943. 30.94418,-97.53634: Site of Thomas Arnold High School. Dr. Samuel J. Jones (1857-1918) and his wife, Charlotte Hallaran Jones (d. 1904), established Thomas Arnold High School on this site in 1890. 30.94455,-97.5329: George Washington Baines House. Built in the 1860s, this house was the residence of the Rev. George Washington Baines (1809-83) from 1870 to 1883. 30.9465,-97.5368: Davis Mill. Built in 1864 by William A. Davis; first stone mill with carding machine in this vicinity. A sawmill and gin were added in 1866. 30.94653,-97.53733: First Baptist Church of Salado. A Baptist revival was held on the banks of Salado Creek as early as 1854. 30.94703,-97.534: M. H. Denman Cabin. M.H. Denman built cabin 1867 (15 mi. NW), of handhewn, square cedar logs joined by wooden pegs; has fireplace of native stone; restored 1955. Recorded Texas Historic Landmark, 1968. #3161
30.94732,-97.53238: Twelve Oaks. Twelve Oaks, 1867-69. Greek Revival mansion built of stone from adjacent land, for B.D. McKie, Texas doctor who fought and was wounded in Mexican and Civil wars. 30.94821,-97.53714: Louisa Adeline (Addie) Barton. 30.94872,-97.53692: Norton-Orgain House. Built about 1872 by Edward R.A. Buckles, this I-plan vernacular house exhibits Classical and Victorian detailing. 30.94917,-97.537: Home of Wellborn Barton. Home of Wellborn Barton 1821-1883; Pioneer physician of this region. For many years a trustee of Salado College, built 1866. (John Hendrickson, Contractor) Old military road and Chisholm cattle trail passed here. #316

30.95232,-97.53646: Salado Church of Christ. Founded in March 1859, this congregation first met in a brush arbor on the north bank of Salado Creek. The first two elders were James Anderson and J.W. 30.95232,-97.75533: Sharp Cemetery and Rock Creek Baptist Church of Christ. Emily LeSeur Haynes Sharp (1824-1880) came to Texas from Alabama with her first husband, William Glenn Haynes. 30.95457,-97.53509: Capt. Robert Bonner Halley Home. N/A #2343
30.9566,-97.53729: West Salado Cemetery. Located in an area populated by former slaves following the Civil War, this cemetery dates to the 1870s. 30.95905,-97.71918: Youngsport. In January 1846, Francis L. Mudd received one-third of a league of land in this area along the Lampasas River. 30.95946,-97.53301: Fowler House. Built 1872 by Josiah Fowler, a settler from Tennessee, Confederate veteran, co-editor of "Fowler's Arithmetic", and a college teacher. Recorded Texas Historic Landmark, 1968 #2044
30.96333,-97.90633: Gillum Cemetery. Absolom Barton Gillum (1836-1923) and his wife, Hannah Emmaline, arrived in Texas from Alabama in 1872. The Gillum Cemetery Association maintains this historic cemetery, a reminder of the area's pioneer ancestors. #17318
30.96657,-97.7802: McBryde Cemetery. Mancel T. McBryde (1821-1896), who brought his family here from Georgia in the early 1860s, began this family cemetery in 1885 upon the death of his wife, Jane W. 30.98525,-97.71699: Live Oak Cemetery. 30.98579,-97.9259: Oakalla. The first settlers in this rich farm and ranch land arrived in the 1850s. Oakalla Post Office was established May 19, 1879. 30.98913,-97.83052: Maxdale Cemetery. Established in the 1860s to serve the rural community of Pleasant Grove, this cemetery is one of the oldest in Bell County. 30.99019,-97.82985: Maxdale Bridge.
